overview: This imported “Celts” layer mostly covers Iron Age Britain and Ireland, where many distinct communities shared some artistic traditions and connections with continental Europe. They were not one Celtic empire, and classical authors did not explicitly call the islanders Celts. The map also adds a continental patch in its 200 BCE snapshot. These changing shapes are an unreliable cultural shorthand, not precise ethnic or political borders.

periods.title: Connected Iron Age communities
periods.summary: The displayed centuries include farming settlements, regional centres and growing overseas connections, with strong local differences.

sections.title: Homes and the work of feeding a family

items.text: At Danebury in Hampshire, roundhouses housed people while separate store buildings and pits held grain. Keeping a harvest safe mattered as much as growing it: the site’s interpretation identifies grain as a particularly valuable resource. The hillfort enclosed a working farming community, not merely a refuge for soldiers.

Danebury’s inhabitants kept sheep and cattle, wove woollen cloth and made leather goods. They needed other areas for iron, tin, copper, salt, shale and stone. The site’s interpreters suggest grain and woollen products went out in exchange. A defended hilltop could still depend on its neighbours.

At Glastonbury Lake Village, in the last centuries BCE, houses stood on wet ground among reeds and open water. Preserved willow or hazel wall posts were surprisingly slim, about 38 millimetres across. Their woven construction seems to have helped the houses hold together, rather like the strength of a basket.

Some Glastonbury walls were decorated by pressing an ammonite fossil into wet daub, the clay mixture covering the walls. The floors had wooden foundations beneath layers of clay. A prehistoric household could have patterned walls, even though its decorating supplies looked rather different from a modern tin of paint.

Glastonbury homes had central hearths, sometimes with a small bread oven beside them. Wooden buckets, turned bowls and bentwood boxes joined pottery containers. Looms and rotary querns belonged to household work: cloth and ground grain required skill, equipment and repeated effort close to home.

Around Maiden Castle in Dorset, people grew wheat, barley, peas or beans and plants of the cabbage family. Managed woodland provided fuel and building materials. The settlement’s impressive banks depended on a surrounding landscape of fields and useful trees to keep its households going.

Dogs at Maiden Castle helped with herding, guarding, hunting and protecting sheep from wolves. Some people also owned horses and perhaps carts. Animals were part of work and security as well as food production; a household’s useful equipment could include a very alert pair of ears.

At Doogarrymore in County Roscommon, two wooden cart wheels dating to the fourth century BCE were found with a bog trackway. Wet ground preserved things that usually decay. Travelling across difficult country could require a deliberately built route, not just a driver hoping the wheels would stay above the mud.

Two gold collars deposited at Ardnaglug in County Roscommon came from the Rhineland during the third century BCE. Local makers then developed their own versions of the flowing La Tène style. Imported ornaments and regional craftsmanship show that Ireland participated in wider artistic networks while producing distinctive work.

The Broighter hoard from County Derry includes a richly decorated gold collar, other neck ornaments, and miniature models of a boat and cauldron. Such precious objects reveal extraordinary metalworking. Their deposition may have had a religious purpose, but the particular intentions of the people who left them are not written down.

The preserved people found at Oldcroghan and Clonycavan in Ireland date broadly to 400 to 200 BCE. Museum researchers used scans and dietary, tissue and disease analyses to investigate them. The bog preserved evidence about individual bodies that is usually missing from ordinary graves.

Clonycavan’s surviving hair was piled high and held with imported resin, according to archaeologist Melanie Giles’s discussion of the research. Personal appearance could involve carefully prepared materials from far away. This is evidence about one person’s hairstyle, rather than a compulsory haircut for everyone labelled Celtic.

A gold coin from southern England, dated by the British Museum to about 40 to 25 BCE, reads “COMMIOS”. This is the Celtic form of the ruler’s name, usually written “Commius” in English, using Roman letters. It is a name rather than a sentence, but it is an actual surviving inscription from before Rome’s conquest.

ending.text: The map’s endpoint just before the Common Era marks no general disappearance. Rome invaded Britain in 43 CE and transformed the areas it conquered, while Ireland and northern Scotland remained outside lasting Roman control. Communities, languages and artistic traditions changed over centuries; modern Celtic identities have their own continuing histories.
